content: This Cochrane review is one of three that investigates the use of telephone-based interventions in HIV/AIDS services. Despite the preventability of HIV infection, a significant number of new cases continue to occur, highlighting the need for more effective prevention strategies. Telephone-based interventions, delivered via landline or mobile phones, have the potential to enhance the delivery of HIV prevention measures by saving time, reducing costs, and improving accessibility. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of HIV prevention interventions delivered through voice calls to HIV-negative individuals. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-randomized controlled trials, controlled before-and-after studies, and interrupted time series studies. These studies compared telephone-delivered HIV prevention interventions to standard care, regardless of participants' demographic characteristics or the settings in which the interventions were implemented. The search strategy involved a comprehensive review of multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, MEDLINE, PubMed Central, EMBASE, PsycINFO, and others, covering the period from 1980 to June 2011. Grey literature sources, such as Dissertation Abstracts International and the Global Health database, were also searched. Two independent reviewers screened citations, assessed study quality, and extracted data, with a third reviewer resolving any disagreements. The primary outcomes assessed were knowledge about HIV/AIDS, behavioral changes, healthcare utilization, and clinical outcomes. Secondary outcomes included user and provider perspectives, economic outcomes, and adverse events. Out of 14,717 citations, only one study met the inclusion criteria. This RCT was conducted in South Africa between August 2007 and May 2008 and involved 274 female participants, including girls, who had received post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) following sexual assault. Participants were randomized into two groups: a telephone support group (n=136) and a control group (n=138). The control group received standard care, which included an interactive information session, but no further contact from study staff. The telephone support group received the same standard care along with regular phone calls from a counselor during the 28-day PEP regimen. The study found no significant difference in PEP adherence between the intervention group (38.2%) and the control group (31.9%) (P=0.13). Similarly, there were no significant differences between the groups in terms of reading a pamphlet (P=0.006), failure to return for medication (P=0.42), or depression rates (P=0.72). However, the use of a diary was significantly higher in the telephone support group (78.8%) compared to the control group (69.9%) (P=0.001). No adverse events were reported. The study did not provide data on participants' or providers' evaluations of the intervention or on economic outcomes. The authors noted that the study had a moderate risk of bias. The authors concluded that the single RCT included in this review, conducted in a high-risk population in an upper-middle-income country with high HIV prevalence, did not demonstrate improved adherence to PEP through telephone support. However, the generalizability of these findings to other settings and populations remains uncertain. The review emphasizes the need for high-quality evidence from diverse settings to assess the effectiveness of telephone-based interventions for PEP support and other HIV prevention strategies.
